subtype: People who feel body signals differently [Observer]
passage:
Monday. Nandini came home to find her flatmate Trisha pale and shaky at her desk. "When did you last eat?" Nandini asked. Trisha blinked. "Oh. I don't know." Nandini sighed, a little annoyed. "How can you not know you're hungry?"
Wednesday. Over tea, Trisha explained quietly. "I'm autistic. For me hunger is often very faint until suddenly it's huge. Same with feeling cold. It's not that I'm careless." Nandini felt her face go hot. She'd been blaming Trisha for weeks.
The next Saturday. They set up a shared routine: lunch together at one on weekends, a phone reminder on weekdays, a bowl of nuts by Trisha's laptop. Nandini also stopped commenting when Trisha wore a jumper in summer.
"Thanks for getting it," Trisha said. Nandini smiled. "Thanks for telling me."

qa.q: What did they put by Trisha's laptop?
qa.a: They put a bowl of nuts by Trisha's laptop.

qa.q: What did Nandini feel after Trisha explained?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face going hot, realising she had been blaming Trisha for weeks.

qa.q: What practical steps helped instead of blame?
qa.a: A shared lunch routine, phone reminders and snacks nearby, so Trisha didn't have to rely on faint hunger signals.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt when Nandini asked how she could not know?
qa.a: Trisha may have felt misunderstood and a little hurt, as if she were being called careless.

grounding: It shows a flatmate learning that some people feel hunger and cold more faintly, and replacing blame with routines and reminders.

subtype: People who feel body signals differently [Observer]
passage:
Sharmila, you asked why I never tease Ronak on our team about his headphones. Let me, Vaibhav, tell you about my nephew, Dev.
When Dev was small, a scraped knee would make him scream as if his leg were broken, and a scratchy label could ruin his whole day. My brother used to say, "Stop the drama." I said it too, I'm ashamed to say.
Then, when Dev was nine, a doctor explained that Dev feels some body sensations much more strongly than most people. It wasn't drama. The pain was real, just louder for him.
That changed everything. We cut out labels, kept his routines steady, and when he was hurt, we believed him first.
Dev is twenty now, studying music. Last Diwali he told me, "You were the first one to stop saying I was faking."

qa.q: What is Dev studying now?
qa.a: Dev is studying music.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about having called Dev dramatic?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels ashamed, looking back, of saying "Stop the drama" to a child whose pain was real.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vaibhav's story, and what changed after it?
qa.a: The doctor's explanation that Dev felt sensations more strongly; after that the family cut out labels, kept routines steady and believed Dev first.

qa.q: How might Dev have felt when adults told him to stop the drama?
qa.a: Dev probably felt hurt and alone, since his pain was real but nobody believed him.

grounding: It shows an adult who learned that a nephew feels pain and sensations more intensely, and replaced blame with belief and steady routines.

passage: The power cut started at nine and lasted all day, on the very day Seema had her project deadline. Lavanya, her flatmate, noticed Seema typing furiously on her laptop's last battery, then on her phone, not stopping. At six Seema suddenly burst into tears and snapped, 'Everything is wrong!' Lavanya asked when she'd last eaten. Seema blinked. 'I… don't know.' Seema is autistic and has told Lavanya before that she often doesn't feel hunger until she's shaky. Lavanya felt a flash of annoyance at being snapped at, then let it go. It wasn't carelessness. She made cheese toast on the gas stove and set it beside Seema. Later, when the lights were back, they set two phone reminders for Seema's meals on busy days, and Seema said, 'Thank you for not being cross.'

qa.q: When did the power cut start?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What did Lavanya feel when Seema snapped?
qa.a: Lavanya felt a flash of annoyance, then understanding.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that avoided blaming Seema?
qa.a: She remembered that Seema often does not feel hunger, made her food and helped set meal reminders.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when Lavanya asked about food?
qa.a: She probably felt surprised and then relieved to realise why she felt so bad.

grounding: Shows an observer understanding that a neurodivergent flatmate feels hunger faintly, and using food and reminders instead of blame.

passage: Vikas noticed that his colleague Sarita, at the Pune office, often worked straight through lunch and by four was pale and shaky, snapping at the printer. At first he thought she was just a workaholic. One day she mentioned, matter-of-factly, that she was neurodivergent and that she barely felt hunger until it hit her all at once. Vikas felt a bit ashamed of how he'd judged her. The next week he suggested something casual. 'A few of us are starting a one o'clock lunch walk. Want a reminder?' Sarita laughed. 'Yes, please. My stomach won't remind me.' They set a team calendar alert for one o'clock. Most days she came along. Her afternoons steadied, and she started setting her own water reminders too.

qa.q: What time is the team lunch walk?
qa.a: One o'clock.

qa.q: What did Vikas feel after Sarita explained?
qa.a: He felt a bit ashamed of how he had judged her as a workaholic.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that respected how Sarita's body works?
qa.a: He suggested a casual lunch walk with a shared calendar reminder instead of blaming her.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel about the reminder?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and supported, since her stomach does not remind her.

grounding: Shows an observer learning that a neurodivergent colleague feels hunger faintly, and using routines and reminders instead of blaming her.

passage:
'Hansa, you left the wedding hall again. Mummy's upset.'
'Mehak, the drums were inside my chest. The lights were like needles. I had to get out.'
'It's just music. Everyone else is fine.'
'I'm not everyone else.' Hansa's hands were shaking. 'You know I feel things louder. My body goes into panic before my head can catch up.'
Mehak was quiet. She had forgotten, or maybe never really listened. 'I'm sorry. I thought you were being difficult.'
'I'm not trying to be.'
'What would help?'
'Ten minutes outside every hour. And my headphones during the baraat.'
'Okay. I'll tell Mummy, and I'll come out with you next time.'
Hansa let out a long breath. 'Thank you for asking.'

qa.q: What did Hansa say the lights felt like?
qa.a: Like needles.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling after Hansa explained?
qa.a: Mehak felt sorry and a little ashamed for thinking Hansa was being difficult.

qa.q: What routine did they agree on to help Hansa?
qa.a: Ten minutes outside every hour and headphones during the baraat, with Mehak explaining to Mummy.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Mehak asked what would help?
qa.a: She felt relieved and understood, letting out a long breath.

grounding: Shows an observer learning that her sister feels sound and emotion in the body more intensely, and using routines instead of blame.

subtype: People who feel body signals differently [Observer]
passage: For months I thought my colleague Abhinav was just careless about lunch. I'm Zeenat, and I sat opposite him in the design team. He'd work straight through till four, then suddenly go pale and shaky, and once he snapped at the intern over a font. I'll admit I rolled my eyes and said, "Just eat when you're hungry, na?" He looked at me, tired. "I don't really feel hungry until it's too late. My body's signals come in very quiet. I'm neurodivergent, and it's common for people like me." I felt awful. After that he set a phone reminder for one o'clock, and I started knocking on his desk when I went for lunch. No lecture, just "Coming?" Most days he comes. The four o'clock crashes have nearly stopped.

qa.q: What time did Abhinav set a phone reminder for?
qa.a: For one o'clock.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel after Abhinav explained, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat felt awful and a bit ashamed for rolling eyes and blaming him for a signal he couldn't easily feel.

qa.q: What support works for Abhinav without blaming him?
qa.a: A phone reminder at one o'clock and a friendly knock on the desk for lunch, with no lecture.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt when Zeenat said "Just eat when you're hungry"?
qa.a: He likely felt tired and misunderstood, blamed for missing a signal his body sends only faintly.

grounding: Shows a colleague learning that a neurodivergent coworker feels hunger faintly, and respecting this with reminders and routine instead of blame.
